Pittsburgh compound B (a radiolabelled benzothiazole compound that binds to amyloid-β plaques in the brain) binds with high affinity to the brain tissue of Alzheimer's patients in most cases, but not in one case.
we found that the Pittsburgh compound B (3H-PI) binding to the cerebral cortex of an Alzheimer’s disease (AD) patient with heavy amyloid deposition was significantly diminished.

a patient with end-stage Alzheimer’s dementia and extensive cerebral β-amyloids had substantially diminished high-affinitity binding of the Pittsburgh compound B (3H-PIBB) to cortical homogenate and unfixed cryo-sections, and that this PIB-refractivity was associated with a distinct pattern of Aβ peptide oligomers and truncations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular and biochemical mechanisms underlying PIB binding to Aβ, with the goal of improving the accuracy of in vivo imaging of Aβ in the brains of living patients.
the development and application of new technologies to study the pathobiology of neurodegenerative disorders.
understanding the molecular basis for the differential binding of PIB to cerebral Aβ deposits in AD patients.

this is an atypical case of Alzheimer’s Disease, and the findings are of interest but do not change the general understanding of the disease.
the patient described in this report had a variant form of AD with a distinctive pattern of Aβ oligomerization, which was not detected with 3H- PIB.
PIB binding to cortical tissue from the AD case was substantially diminished, but the reasons for this remain to be determined.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PIB binding site in the brain is a complex, dynamic, and polymorphic entity.
PIB binding to cerebral β-aminoyd is not always stoichiometric and can be deficient in some cases of Alzheimer’s disease.
the binding of PIB in AD patients is not always stoichiometric and that the presence of PIB binding in AD patients is necessary but not sufficient for the presence of AD pathology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of PIB as a biomarker for AD is still evolving.
